lead: Friction is the force at a contact that opposes sliding, or the tendency to slide. It exists because real surfaces are rough at small scale and atoms attract across the contact. Dry friction follows simple laws: the friction force opposes impending motion, and its maximum is μN, where μ is the coefficient of friction and N is the normal reaction. Engineers use these laws to size brakes, clutches, ramps and bolt threads, and to check that a ladder, block or machine will not slip.
prereq: You need: equilibrium of a particle and free-body diagrams from Unit 1 and Unit 2; the free-body habit is used again in frames and machines.

blocks.text: Dry friction acts at the contact between two surfaces that touch without oil or grease. Push a heavy box on a floor with a small horizontal force P. The box does not move: static friction F balances P. Increase P and F grows, but only up to a limit. At the limit the box is about to slide; this is limiting friction. Once it slides, kinetic friction acts, and it is smaller than the limiting value.
Static friction is a response, not a fixed value. It takes only the value needed for equilibrium, up to its limit.

items: Friction acts along the common tangent, opposite the impending or actual sliding.
Limiting static friction is proportional to the normal reaction: F<sub>max</sub> = μ<sub>s</sub>N. μ<sub>s</sub> is the static coefficient; N is the normal reaction in newtons.
Kinetic friction is F<sub>k</sub> = μ<sub>k</sub>N. μ<sub>k</sub> is the kinetic coefficient. Usually μ<sub>k</sub> < μ<sub>s</sub>, so kinetic friction is smaller than limiting static friction.
For ordinary hard surfaces, friction is nearly independent of apparent contact area and of low sliding speed.

blocks.text: Some syllabi call these Coulomb's laws of friction.

Divide the limiting friction by the normal reaction to get the coefficient of friction. For static limiting friction μ<sub>s</sub> = F<sub>max</sub>/N; for sliding μ<sub>k</sub> = F<sub>k</sub>/N. Both coefficients have no unit.
μ<sub>s</sub> = F<sub>max</sub> / N,  φ = tan⁻¹ μ<sub>s</sub>
blocks.where: μ<sub>s</sub> is the static coefficient (no unit); F<sub>max</sub> is limiting friction in N; N is normal reaction in N; φ is the angle of friction in degrees.

blocks.text: The angle of friction is a geometric way to say the same thing. The resultant of N and F<sub>max</sub> makes angle φ with N, so tan φ = F<sub>max</sub>/N = μ<sub>s</sub>. A rough surface with μ<sub>s</sub>=0.4 has φ=21.8°.

For a block on an incline, the steepest angle at which it stays put is the angle of repose α = tan⁻¹ μs. The angle of repose is measured by tilting the surface until motion is just about to start. On an incline N = W cos θ, not W; the full treatment is in block on a rough incline.
Use the laws in a fixed order so you do not mix static and kinetic friction.

items: Draw the free body diagram. Show N perpendicular to the surface and friction along the surface, opposing the impending motion.
Find N from equilibrium in the direction perpendicular to the surface. Horizontal floor: N = W. Incline: N = W cos θ.
Compute the limiting static friction F<sub>max</sub> = μ<sub>s</sub>N.
Compare the applied tangential force P with F<sub>max</sub>. If P ≤ F<sub>max</sub>, the body is static and F = P. If P > F<sub>max</sub>, it slides and F = μ<sub>k</sub>N.
Use μ<sub>s</sub> for the angle of friction while the body is at the limit; use μ<sub>k</sub> only when it is already sliding.

blocks.text: The most common mistake is to write F = μN while the body is still static below the limit. Static friction can be any value from zero up to μ<sub>s</sub>N. It equals the applied tangential force until that force reaches the limit. Check the direction last: friction always opposes relative motion or its tendency, not the applied force by name.

figure.caption: Static friction rises one-for-one with applied force to 80 N; after the block starts to move, kinetic friction drops to 60 N and stays there.

spec.aria: A graph of friction force against applied force: static friction rises with applied force to 80 N, then kinetic friction drops to 60 N.

examples.question: A 200 N block rests on a horizontal floor. The coefficients are μ<sub>s</sub> = 0.4 and μ<sub>k</sub> = 0.3. Find (a) the limiting friction, (b) the friction when the applied horizontal force is 60 N, and (c) the angle of friction.
steps: The floor is horizontal, so the normal reaction balances the weight: N = W = 200 N.
The applied force is 60 N, which is less than 80 N. The block is static, so friction balances the applied force: F = 60 N.
The kinetic coefficient is not used because the block is not sliding. The number μ<sub>k</sub>N = 60 N is a coincidence of these data.
Angle of friction: φ = tan⁻¹ μ<sub>s</sub> = tan⁻¹ 0.4 = 21.8°.
examples.answer: Limiting friction = 80 N; friction at 60 N applied = 60 N; angle of friction φ = 21.8°.
examples.check:
import math
W = 200.0
mu_s = 0.4
mu_k = 0.3
P = 60.0
N = W
F_limit = mu_s * N
F_static = P
phi = math.degrees(math.atan(mu_s))
print(f'{F_limit:.0f}')
print(f'{F_static:.0f}')
print(f'{phi:.1f}')

traps: Using μ<sub>k</sub> while the block is still static. Check P against μ<sub>s</sub>N first.
Using N = W on an incline. Resolve perpendicular to the surface; there N = W cos θ.
Writing F = μN for a static body below the limit. Static friction equals the applied tangential force, not μ<sub>s</sub>N.
Dropping units or treating μ as a force. μ is a pure ratio; friction is in newtons.
Pointing friction along the applied force instead of opposite impending motion.

quiz.q: State the law for limiting static friction.
quiz.a: Limiting static friction equals μ<sub>s</sub>N, acts opposite impending sliding, and is proportional to the normal reaction.

quiz.q: Why is kinetic friction usually smaller than limiting static friction?
quiz.a: At rest the junctions have time to grow and bond, so breaking them needs the larger limiting value. Once sliding starts, junctions are made and broken quickly with less time for bonding and interlocking, so μ<sub>k</sub> < μ<sub>s</sub>.

quiz.q: A 500 N block rests on a horizontal floor with μ<sub>s</sub> = 0.35 and μ<sub>k</sub> = 0.25. A horizontal force of 150 N is applied. Find the friction force.
quiz.a: N = 500 N. F<sub>max</sub> = 0.35 × 500 = 175 N. Since 150 N < 175 N, the block is static and F = 150 N.

quiz.q: A block rests on a rough incline of angle 20° with μ<sub>s</sub> = 0.45. With no other force, will it slide?
quiz.a: Angle of repose α = tan⁻¹ 0.45 = 24.2°. Since 20° < 24.2°, the block does not slide.

quiz.q: A horizontal force exactly equal to μ<sub>s</sub>N is applied to a block at rest. Describe the motion immediately after.
quiz.a: At exactly the limit the block is about to slide. Any extra force makes it slide; friction then falls to μ<sub>k</sub>N, so the net force becomes positive and the block accelerates.

quiz.q: A student uses N = W to find limiting friction on an incline. Is the result safe or unsafe? Explain.
quiz.a: Unsafe. On an incline N = W cos θ, which is less than W. Using W in place of N overestimates the friction limit and may predict no slip when slip actually occurs.

quiz.q: Give one difference between coefficient and angle of friction.
quiz.a: Coefficient μ is the ratio F/N, with no unit. Angle φ is the angle whose tan is μ, measured in degrees.

beyond: Not for exam. In machine design, friction coefficients are measured for each pair of materials and finishes; tables give only a starting range. Tribology studies friction, wear and lubrication at contacts. Brake and clutch design depends on a stable μ, while earthquake engineering studies stick-slip at faults. Search next: Coulomb friction, Stribeck curve, tribology, stick-slip.
